brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about gambling?
brief.answer:
The strongest, most decision-relevant finding in the parliamentary record is that gambling harm is now national in scale: Australians spent a record $244.3 billion on gambling in 2022-23, or $11,859 per person, and a 2022 federal parliamentary inquiry found that four out of five gamblers were at risk of harm. That inquiry heard testimony of financial ruin, substance abuse, homelessness, domestic violence and mental illness, and one committee member quoted a constituent describing 18-year-olds with existing gambling addictions amid a “constant bombardment” of ads during family shows and sport. A second point of wide agreement is the Murphy report, “You win some, you lose more,” produced three years ago with 31 unanimous recommendations across party lines, including phasing out online gambling advertising. Numerous speakers have since noted that the government did not respond to that report, let alone implement its recommendations, leaving what one member called “a thousand days of inaction.”

On the question of what has actually happened over time, the record shows some earlier progress followed by a prolonged stall. Coalition speakers highlighted that in 2018 their government banned gambling ads during live sport, including a five-minute window either side, legislated the BetStop national self-exclusion register, and prohibited betting companies from offering sign-up inducements. In contrast, current government representatives say they are delivering the “strongest ever reforms” to tackle gambling harm by making ads easier to switch off online, weakening the connection between wagering and sport, reducing children’s exposure to ads, and strengthening inducement rules. But opposition and crossbench critics dispute that framing, describing the government’s bill as “pathetic” and as ignoring most Murphy recommendations, while evidence continues to emerge such as children hearing Sportsbet ads on Spotify between Disney songs.

The sharpest disagreement is over why reform has stalled. Several speakers argue the gambling lobby is the obstacle: in the last five years companies including Sportsbet, Tabcorp and the Australian Hotels Association donated $4 million to the Labor Party and more than $2 million to the coalition, which one member called “having a bet each way” to stop parliament acting. Another said the gambling lobby is “louder and richer” and “far more present in these halls than the people being hurt by gambling.” A contrasting view warns against singling out individuals with gambling addiction and instead calls the state-level poker machine expansion an obscenity, citing the Liverpool council decision to sell the RSL Memorial Swimming Complex to Canterbury Bankstown Leagues Club for a $100 million hotel complex with at least 1,000 poker machines. The record also includes calls for a royal commission and inquiry into links between gambling, Crown casino, money laundering and corruption, alongside proposals to reduce account verification times from 21 days to 72 hours, ban live odds promotion at venues and during game broadcasts, prohibit gambling advertising in children’s viewing times, and create a mandatory code of conduct for wagering advertising.

sections.question: What have MPs said about gambling reform and poker machine regulation?
sections.answer:
Australian parliamentarians have voiced a wide spectrum of positions on gambling reform, from calls for aggressive intervention to warnings about economic fallout. A recurring theme is the tension between public health concerns and the significant revenue and employment generated by the industry.

**The Push for Stronger Regulation and Harm Reduction**

Many MPs have framed problem gambling, particularly poker machine addiction, as a severe social evil requiring urgent, bipartisan action similar to tobacco control. One Labor MP argued that the national parliament must tackle the poker machine industry, which they described as a "virulent social evil," and commended the government's reforms, including mandatory precommitment capability in new machines and a $250 daily ATM withdrawal limit in gaming venues. This MP also criticized the Opposition for being "slippery" on policy and suspected they would ultimately back the "pokies industry" due to significant donations.

Independent and crossbench figures have pushed for even more ambitious measures. Senator Nick Xenophon and Andrew Wilkie have advocated for stronger restraints, with Xenophon introducing the Poker Machine Harm Reduction ($1 Bets and Other Measures) Bill 2012 to regulate machines and reduce harm. Another speaker challenged the government's inconsistency, noting it would work with states on some gambling issues but refused to act on poker machine reform, citing it as a state matter, despite the fact that 100,000 addicts lose $4–5 billion annually.

State-level politicians have also voiced strong criticism. In New South Wales, Greg Piper argued that reforms were only a "small step" and failed to address the root causes of addiction. He highlighted that Australia has 20% of the world's poker machines, with over 94,000 in neighbourhood pubs and clubs, and that problem gambling plays a role in up to 20% of suicides. He called for a drastic reduction in machine numbers, a cap on bet amounts, and the removal of note acceptors, arguing that the industry's quiet acceptance of the bill was a sign it was ineffective.

**The Industry and Economic Concerns**

Opposition to stringent reforms has focused on the economic importance of pubs and clubs and the issue of sovereign risk. A Victorian Liberal MP detailed the sector's contributions: clubs provide 30,000 jobs, have 2.3 million members, and give back $805 million in free or subsidised facilities, while AHA members employ 52,000 people and contribute $4.5 billion to the state's gross product. This MP argued that the government's reforms, announced without consultation, created sovereign risk by changing the rules shortly after entering into 20-year licence agreements. They supported mandatory closing hours but moved an amendment to exempt venues within 3km of the casino, arguing it was unfair to disadvantage them when the casino itself was exempt.

**The Casino Exception and Calls for Consistency**

A major point of contention is the exemption of Crown Casino from certain reforms, such as mandatory closing hours. The Victorian Liberal MP called this "contradictory and hypocritical," given the casino's history of "disgraceful" conduct as found by a royal commission. They argued that venues in direct competition with the casino should not be disadvantaged. Conversely, a government minister defended the reforms, citing significant progress like mandatory 4 am to 10 am closures for venues, slower spin rates, and reduced ATM withdrawals, while acknowledging more work was needed.

**The Role of the Commonwealth and Online Gambling**

The debate also covers the jurisdictional divide. A speaker noted the government's willingness to work with states on some measures but its refusal to act on poker machines, calling this a contradiction. Others have pointed to the rapid growth of online gambling as a critical gap. One MP argued that removing all poker machines would be pointless if online casinos operating from overseas remain unregulated, while another criticised the government's online gambling bill for failing to address advertising, a national self-exclusion database, and the use of credit for online gambling.

**A 2012 Division on Precommitment Deadlines**

A specific parliamentary division in 2012 on the National Gambling Reform Bill showed a narrow split (72–69) on delaying the deadline for precommitment capability in poker machines. The majority, including Labor MPs and independents like Tony Windsor, voted in favour of the delay, while the minority included many Coalition MPs such as Tony Abbott, Malcolm Turnbull, and Scott Morrison.

sections.question: What arguments have been made against tighter gambling regulation, and by whom?
sections.answer: Arguments against tighter gambling regulation have come primarily from coalition members and government representatives, who emphasize personal choice and industry legitimacy. Coalition speakers defended "personal choice and personal responsibility," noting that "millions of Australians have an occasional punt without gambling harm" and that government must respect those choices, while still supporting protections for children and vulnerable Australians. They rejected comparisons to tobacco regulation, arguing the bill is not a ban on gambling but a debate over promotion. Government representatives opposed amendments for a national regulator, arguing gambling regulation is a state responsibility and that their "balanced package" approach—reducing advertising exposure and introducing an opt-out system online—strikes the right balance between a "legitimate industry" and community concerns. A coalition member also criticized the minister's call for more foreign investment in gambling as contradictory to restraint, and another argued investigative processes into Crown Casino should run their course before conclusions are drawn.

sections.question: What has been said about the influence of the gambling industry on politics?
sections.answer:
The gambling industry has exercised pervasive and undue influence over Australian politics, primarily through political donations, lobbying, and privileged access to decision-makers. Gambling-related industries have made over $80 million in political donations in the last two decades, including $1.5 million to political parties in 2023-24, with most going to the Australian Labor Party. The industry has hired 13 third-party lobbying firms to influence parliament, with Responsible Wagering Australia accessing over 100 lobbyists across all jurisdictions. The Grattan Institute found that industries most affected by regulation—gambling, property, and fossil fuels—dominate donations, lobbying contracts, and meetings with senior ministers.

Speakers across the debate, including Greens members and crossbenchers, argued that this influence has directly stalled reform. The Murphy report into gambling harm, released over 1,000 days ago, has not had a single one of its 31 recommendations adopted. Critics attributed this inaction to industry pressure, noting that the Labor Party collected more than $4.4 million in gambling donations over five years, including $1.5 million around the last election. In 2024, at least 19 federal politicians from both Labor and the Coalition accepted gifts from Tabcorp and Sportsbet to attend sporting events, including the Nationals leader and the shadow health minister. The minister responsible for gambling reportedly accepted almost $20,000 in donations to her own election campaign.

The record also highlights the revolving door between politics and the industry: former Labor communications minister Stephen Conroy became CEO of the peak industry body for gambling companies, and former NSW Liberal premier Barry O'Farrell became CEO of Racing Australia. The gambling industry has also sponsored parliamentary groups, particularly the Parliamentary Sports Club, raising integrity concerns. The AFL and NRL each make about $50 million from gambling revenue, and media companies are reliant on gambling advertising, which critics say stifles coverage and reform.

A Greens amendment to ban donations from gambling companies was rejected by the Senate, with 11 votes in favour and 24 against. The amendment noted that major parties had received over $10 million from gambling companies and lobby groups. Speakers argued that this money has "bought significant influence" over the debate on gambling reform bills, with one stating that "the gambling lobby has more influence on the Labor Party than Labor's own members." The racing and gambling industries were also singled out for undue influence in New South Wales politics, including a memorandum of understanding with ClubsNSW protecting poker machine profits and lobbying that exempted the racing industry from gambling advertising reforms.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Gambling Legislation Amendment (Pre-commitment and Carded Play) Bill 2024?
sections.answer:
Debate on the Gambling Legislation Amendment (Pre-commitment and Carded Play) Bill 2024 was sharply partisan in the Victorian Parliament. The bill establishes a framework for mandatory carded play and precommitment on electronic gaming machines, introduces a minimum 3-second spin rate for new machines, and includes anti-money-laundering identity verification measures. Government speakers, including Labor's Minister for Casino, Gaming and Liquor Regulation Melissa Horne and members such as the member for Clarinda, supported it as "landmark gambling reforms" that would "help address gambling harms and prevent money laundering." Labor's member for Eureka and the member for Melton highlighted personal and community harm, with the latter noting record losses of "$3.03 billion" on poker machines in 2023–24. The Greens supported the bill but criticised delays, with Katherine Copsey arguing the reforms "should go further and can too easily be wound back by a change in government."

Opposition speakers from the Liberal and National parties opposed the bill. The member for Euroa claimed it "does not leave room for choice" and would "infringe upon personal freedoms," while the member for Gippsland South argued it would hurt pubs, clubs and RSLs, reduce casual gaming and cause job losses, citing Crown Casino's loss of "a thousand jobs" after carded play was introduced there. The member for Gippsland East raised concerns about border venues and trial locations, asking the government to "please keep out of Gippsland East." The opposition also questioned the evidence base, with the member for Euroa noting that "participation in pokie play has halved from 22 per cent of the population in 2008 to 11 per cent in 2023" and that the highest rates of problem gambling are among bingo and Keno players, not pokies players. The bill was ultimately passed with house amendments ensuring the minister's direction is "subject to parliamentary oversight," and the opposition stated it was "now not opposing it" after initially voting against it.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Greyhound racing and gambling?
sections.answer:
Several parliamentarians across Australian jurisdictions have spoken strongly against greyhound racing, linking it to gambling harm and animal cruelty. In the New South Wales Legislative Council, The Hon. Emma Hurst (Animal Justice Party) moved a bill to ban greyhound racing, arguing the industry "has animal cruelty built into its business model" and that it "only exists because of gambling money." She claimed the industry has repeatedly failed to reform despite being given a "last chance" after the 2015 live baiting scandal, citing ongoing deaths, injuries, and overbreeding, and noted that "commercial greyhound racing is now banned in over 40 US states" and that New Zealand announced a ban by 2026. Hurst also criticised the NSW Government for continuing to fund the industry with taxpayer money.

In the Commonwealth Parliament, a member (unnamed in the passages) criticised the Albanese government's gambling advertising reforms for exempting racing, saying the bill "gives a green light for wagering companies to go all-in on funnelling their marketing budgets into horse and greyhound racing." Another Commonwealth member argued that "horse and greyhound racing lost their social licence years ago" and that the racing exemption exists "purely to sustain what would otherwise be a dead and buried industry." However, a different Commonwealth speaker supported the racing carve-out, stating "wagering has always been intrinsic to racing" and that racing is "enormously important to regional Australia."

In Tasmania, a member praised Liberal Premier Jeremy Rockliff for acknowledging greyhound racing is "an industry built on cruelty, injury, death and wastage" and for planning to end state subsidies by 2029, while criticising the Labor opposition for protecting the industry. In Queensland, a Greens member noted the sport is "banned in New Zealand as of 31 July," in the ACT, and in "forty-four states of the United States," and tabled polling showing "66 per cent" of Queenslanders support ending greyhound racing. In Victoria, a question was asked about why the minister continues to subsidise greyhound racing despite a Parliamentary Budget Office report finding a ban would save the state "almost half a billion dollars over 10 years."

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Gambling Legislation Amendment Bill 2025?
sections.answer:
Debate on the Gambling Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 was sharply partisan. The Liberal–National opposition opposed the bill, with members arguing it introduced "another new big Labor tax on Victorians" through a premium payment on the monitoring licence, which they said would flow through to venues and clubs as higher monitoring and compliance fees. One opposition member, speaking in the Victorian parliament, said the bill lacked detail, created uncertainty about licence terms, and that the government was "desperate to keep their hand in the pockets of venues to prop up their budget." The same member acknowledged one positive: the phasing out of cheques was "largely welcomed" by venues. A Libertarian member also opposed the bill, calling the premium "effectively a new gambling tax" and saying he had promised never to support a tax increase.

Government members in the Victorian parliament strongly defended the bill. The minister, Anthony Carbines, said it would "improve the regulatory framework for gambling in Victoria" and give the government flexibility in future licensing to "yield the best outcomes for the state." Other Labor speakers framed the premium as extracting "value" from licences, with funds going to the Hospitals and Charities Fund to support harm minimisation. One Labor member criticised the opposition for being "stuck in the tax vortex" and ignoring gambling harm, while another said the bill modernised the licensing framework and improved integrity safeguards. The bill also made changes to voluntary exclusion orders at the casino, requiring the operator to issue an exclusion order on request, and removed the need for applications to be witnessed.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Greyhound Racing Industry and gambling?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on greyhound racing and gambling was extensive and sharply critical of the industry. The Hon. Emma Hurst (NSW Legislative Council, Animal Justice Party) moved a bill to ban greyhound racing in New South Wales, arguing the industry "has animal cruelty built into its business model" and that "the only way to end the cruelty is to end the industry." She cited the 2015 Four Corners expose on live baiting, the McHugh inquiry's finding that up to 70 per cent of greyhounds born had been killed as "wastage," and ongoing deaths—including 17 killed and 4,223 injured on NSW tracks in one year, plus at least five dogs killed in a US export program. Hurst claimed the industry "never cleaned up its act after 2015" and that the Minns Labor Government had failed to revoke Greyhound Racing NSW's operating licence despite promising to do so if noncompliance continued.

Other speakers echoed these themes. Abigail Boyd (NSW Legislative Council, The Greens) supported transparency motions and noted Scotland, Wales, Tasmania and Western Australia were moving to ban greyhound racing, while New Zealand had recommitted to a ban by 2026. A Commonwealth speaker (unnamed in the passages) said "Australia stands virtually alone as the global stronghold of the cruel greyhound racing industry" and called for "at least a ban on online gambling on racing." Another Commonwealth speaker criticised the Albanese government's gambling advertising bill as "piss-weak," arguing it exempted racing channels and that "horse and greyhound racing lost their social licence years ago." In contrast, a government-aligned speaker (NSW, Hon. Stephen Lawrence) defended the industry's regulatory framework, noting the Drake inquiry report was being considered and that the Government wanted "the highest standards of governance, integrity and animal welfare" in the industry.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Casino and Gambling Legislation Amendment Bill 2025?
sections.answer:
Debate on the Casino and Gambling Legislation Amendment Bill 2025 in the Victorian Parliament was sharply divided. The Greens opposed the bill, with two Greens members delivering near-identical speeches. They supported its "modest good steps" — such as new powers for the Victorian Gambling and Casino Control Commission (VGCCC) to discipline Crown's "corporate associates" with fines of up to $1 million, and an additional $1 million per day fine for ignoring directions tied to the Melbourne transformation plan — but condemned its delays. They said the bill pushes back key cashless controls, including the $1000 per day cash limit and electronic payment of winnings over $1000, from 1 December 2025 to 1 December 2027, and defers carded play on traditional table games to 2027. One Greens speaker called this "a huge step backwards" that "aids and abets" money laundering by organised crime, citing Victoria Police evidence to the Royal Commission that cash-and-carry laundering at the casino would "happen on a daily basis".

The Liberal–Nationals opposition did not oppose the bill. Its speakers framed the two-year extension as a pragmatic response to technology that "does not exist anywhere in the world" for carded play on traditional tables, noting Crown is investing about $40 million in new technology. They stressed Crown's economic importance as Victoria's largest single employer with around 13,000 staff, and warned that without the extension Crown might have to close traditional table games, risking about 1000 jobs. They also supported the bill's increase in the club gaming machine entitlements cap from 840 to 1260, saying it helps smaller clubs exit the pokies market. Government speakers, including Minister Anthony Carbines, defended the bill as delivering on royal commission reforms, strengthening the regulator, and providing time to "develop, test and roll out cashless technology". One government speaker said the bill "builds on Victoria's record of nation-leading gambling reform".

sections.question: What have MPs said about gambling reform and poker machine regulation since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Debate on gambling reform and poker machine regulation since July 2024 has been extensive and sharply partisan across several Australian parliaments. In the Victorian Legislative Assembly, the Liberal–National opposition criticised the Gambling Legislation Amendment (Pre-commitment and Carded Play) Bill 2024 for setting up a framework rather than fully introducing mandatory carded play, arguing the government was "giving itself a head of power" without parliamentary scrutiny of the details. The opposition also claimed the reforms would harm pubs and clubs, citing Crown Casino's downturn after mandatory carded play, and questioned the evidence base, noting the Victorian Population Gambling and Health Study found only 0.9 per cent of the population experience problem gambling and that participation in pokie play halved from 22 per cent in 2008 to 11 per cent in 2023. The Greens supported the bill but moved amendments to require implementation by 1 December 2027, criticising the lack of a deadline and arguing the trial was duplicative since the technology already operates at Crown Casino. The Greens also advocated for default maximum limits of $100 a day, $500 per month and $5000 per year, slower spin rates of at least 5 seconds, and abolition of the community benefits scheme, which they called "a complete sham". The government minister, Enver Erdogan, said the bill creates a framework for staged implementation and that the government would "revisit the implementation timeline" given technological developments and approaches in bordering jurisdictions, while circulating amendments to ensure ministerial directions are subject to parliamentary scrutiny.

In the New South Wales Parliament, Premier Chris Minns defended his government's record, listing reforms including revoking over 650 exemptions to mandatory shutdown periods, reducing the statewide gaming machine entitlement cap by over 3,000 machines, banning political donations from clubs with gaming machines, reducing cash input limits from $5,000 to $500 for new machines, and investing $100 million in harm minimisation. Opposition member Cate Faehrmann criticised the government for delays, noting pokie losses increased by 8 per cent to $9.3 billion in the past year and that the number of machines increased by 247 on Minns's watch, and she moved an order for papers on the government's response to the independent panel's recommendation for mandatory account-based gaming. Government member Liesl Tesch said the government could not support a bill on returning proceeds of crime from gambling, arguing it was already addressing harm through evidence-based policy and that clubs are vital community centres and employers. In the Commonwealth Parliament, debate on the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026 saw government supporters call it "the strongest action against gambling that Australia has ever seen", while an opponent called it "a cave-in" and "shameful", arguing it did not respond fully to the Murphy report's recommendations.

sections.question: What arguments have been made against tighter gambling regulation, and by whom since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Arguments against tighter gambling regulation appear in the record from several sources. A coalition member in the Victorian Legislative Assembly, debating the Gambling Legislation Amendment (Pre-commitment and Carded Play) Bill 2024, said they were "puzzled" by arguments from the other side, characterising one previous speaker as wanting to "take over and socialise all the lotteries in Victoria or Australia on behalf of government," while asserting "there is this amorphous good about lotteries." In the same Victorian debate, another coalition member said the Liberals and Nationals "always want to support the reduction of gambling harm" but "understand that gambling is a legitimate pastime for many," and that they would "always stand up for our local pubs and community clubs," acknowledging the advocacy of the Australian Hotels Association.

In the Commonwealth Parliament, a senator opposing the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Ban Gambling Ads) Bill 2024 said they had heard coalition members argue at second reading "that there could be unintended consequences that are similar to tobacco regulation," though the senator found those arguments unpersuasive. Separately, a senator speaking on the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026 claimed the gambling industry's case against reform included research commissioned by Responsible Wagering Australia that was presented "as independent market monitoring when it was actually research paid for by the industry peak body," and that the industry argued "Advertising is demonstrably not what contains the offshore market; enforcement is." The same senator also alleged that the gambling lobby's strategy was to say, "Don't look at us. Look over there. Look at pokies, look at lotto... We're not to be regulated first."

sections.question: What has been said about the influence of the gambling industry on politics since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Speakers across multiple parliaments have alleged that the gambling industry exerts pervasive and corrupting influence over Australian politics, particularly over the federal Labor government. In the Commonwealth Parliament, Senator Sarah Hanson-Young (Greens) claimed the industry "has long had a powerful lobbying influence in Australia," using political donations, sponsorships and lobbying to shape policy, and that "gambling related industries have made more than $80 million in political donations over the last two decades alone," with $1.5 million in 2023-24 mostly going to Labor. She said it has been "more than a thousand days" since the Murphy report was released and the government has adopted "not even one" of its 31 recommendations, attributing this to industry influence. Senator Hanson-Young also cited former Labor minister Stephen Conroy becoming CEO of the peak industry body and former NSW Liberal premier Barry O'Farrell leading Racing Australia as examples of revolving-door lobbying. Another Commonwealth speaker, Senator Sarah Hanson-Young again, claimed "the gambling lobby has more influence on the Labor Party than Labor's own members," and that Labor and coalition MPs received "$245,000 in free sports tickets" from organisations opposing a gambling ad ban, with the Prime Minister personally accepting close to $29,000 and Peter Dutton over $21,000.

In the New South Wales Parliament, Ms Cate Faehrmann (Greens) moved a motion for an inquiry into the gambling industry's political influence, stating that "the gambling industry is dramatically over-represented in every measure of political influence compared to its contribution to the economy." She accused the Minns Labor Government of "cosying up to the clubs industry" and refusing to implement mandatory account-based gaming recommended by an independent panel, noting poker machine losses rose 8 per cent to $9.3 billion in the past year and the number of machines increased by 247. The motion was agreed to. In the Commonwealth Parliament, a speaker (unnamed in the passage) said the government released its response to a key gambling report "on the afternoon of the budget" to bury it, and that the industry's "almost $3 million in donations to the major parties over the last decade" had "paid off." Another Commonwealth speaker, Senator Hanson-Young, described the gambling industry as "so deeply embedded in our politics it feels like trying to pry open steel with our bare hands," while a further speaker claimed the Prime Minister had "capitulated to vested interests" and "actively engaged in watering down reform" despite 80 per cent of Australians wanting a ban on gambling ads. A government-aligned speaker defended the record, noting BetStop was established in 2023, seven additional measures were introduced at the close of 2024, and the Prime Minister announced 11 more measures in April, with "hopefully more to come."

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did parliament argue about gambling between 1993 and 2009?
eras.answer:
Debate on gambling in the Commonwealth Parliament between 1993 and 2009 centred heavily on interactive and online gambling, with sharp partisan division over how to handle it. Government speakers, including members of the Liberal and National parties, argued for bans and moratoriums to prevent the spread of gambling. One government-aligned speaker said the Interactive Gambling Bill 2001 was about taking "strong and decisive action to protect Australian families from the further spread of problem gambling," citing Productivity Commission findings that around 290,000 Australians were problem gamblers. Another government speaker claimed the opposition wanted "a poker machine in every lounge room," while the Nationals "want to make families stronger and keep them together." A supporter of the Interactive Gambling (Moratorium) Bill 2000 described it as "a breathing space, and a sensible breathing space" to examine the consequences of online gambling, and another said it would "protect the vulnerable and the young."

Opposition and some crossbench speakers attacked these measures as hypocritical and unworkable. A Labor speaker moved a second reading amendment condemning the government for "introducing an unworkable, internally inconsistent and hypocritical bill," arguing that a ban would not work and would drive users to "unregulated offshore online gambling sites." Another Labor speaker said the government's approach was "based on hypocrisy and the pretence that the attempted banning by the government of online gambling will actually solve the problem," and that the result was "a hypocritical, unworkable dog's breakfast." A Labor speaker also criticised the government for singling out online gambling while ignoring poker machines, saying "the hypocrisy knows no bounds" and that the government was making a judgment that it was "fine for people in some other country to gamble on these sites" but not for Australians. One speaker supporting the moratorium acknowledged the social costs, noting that problem gamblers "account for one-third of all gambling expenditure" and that "levels of problem gambling are linked to the level of accessibility and type of gambling products."

The record also shows debate over specific amendments. The Interactive Gambling Amendment Bill 2001 was introduced to fix an unintended consequence where the advertising ban could catch land-based casinos that also offered lawful interactive gambling services to overseas customers. A government speaker said the amendment provided "a regulation making power" to exempt certain advertisements, while a Labor speaker said the bill "only serves to further highlight the unworkability and hypocrisy of the government's approach." A government speaker in that debate accused Labor of being "soft on Internet gambling just as they are soft on drugs, soft on crime," while a Labor speaker responded that the government's approach was not the most effective way to address the social harm. The record is limited to these exchanges on interactive gambling policy; it does not canvass other forms of gambling debate in that period.

eras.question: How did parliament argue about gambling between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016, Greyhound Racing Bill 2017 and Betting Tax Amendment (Point of Consumption) Bill 2018.
eras.answer:
Debate on gambling in New South Wales between 2016 and 2018 was sharply contested, centring on the greyhound racing ban and its repeal, and on the design of a new point-of-consumption betting tax. In 2016 the NSW Government passed the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016, which Mr LUKE FOLEY (Auburn, Labor) sought to repeal immediately, accusing the Government of a "con" for delaying repeal: "It was urgent to ban greyhound racing. Why is it not urgent to repeal that awful piece of law and take it off the statute books?" The Hon. DUNCAN GAY (NSW Legislative Council) admitted the ban was a mistake: "for all the right reasons, we got it damn wrong." The Greens opposed the repeal, with Dr MEHREEN FARUQI (NSW Legislative Council) and others lodging a formal protest against the Greyhound Racing Bill 2017, citing "entrenched animal neglect and cruelty, dog drugging and the breeding and killing of tens of thousands of greyhounds for the purposes of gambling."

The Betting Tax Amendment (Point of Consumption) Bill 2018, introducing a 10 per cent tax on wagering revenue from NSW bets, drew a different set of arguments. Mr RYAN PARK (Keira, Labor) led the Opposition in supporting the tax but moving amendments for revenue to be distributed by market share rather than the 1998 Racing Inter-Code Deed, and for an independent review after 12 months. Mr PHILIP DONATO (Orange, Shooters, Fishers and Farmers) argued the greyhound industry contributed "approximately 23 per cent of market share revenue but only receives 13 per cent in return", calling that "disproportionate and unfair". The Hon. ROBERT BORSAK (NSW Legislative Council, Shooters, Fishers and Farmers) moved to cut the rate to 8 per cent, claiming the TAB and thoroughbred industry wanted to "kill the greyhound racing industry once and for all". By contrast, Mr JUSTIN FIELD (NSW Legislative Council, Greens) moved to raise the rate to 15 per cent, arguing gambling taxes should be increased. Mr ALEX GREENWICH (Sydney, Greens) in the Legislative Assembly also backed 15 per cent and criticised the 2 per cent rebate to racing as "reinvested in gambling". Treasurer Mr DOMINIC PERROTTET (Hawkesbury, Liberal) defended 10 per cent as "the considered, moderate middle", rejecting both the Greens' 15 per cent and the Shooters' 8 per cent.

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did parliament argue about gambling between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included SkyCity Adelaide, Casino Legislation Amendment Bill 2022 and Gambling Regulation Amendment (Wagering and Betting Tax) Bill 2021.
eras.answer:
Debate on gambling in Victoria between 2020 and mid-2024 was extensive and largely framed around licensing reform, taxation, and harm minimisation, with recurring partisan friction over process and fairness. In the Victorian Parliament, the **Gambling Regulation Amendment Bill 2023** drew contributions from government and opposition members alike. Government speakers, including the member for Narre Warren South, defended the bill as "in essence technical changes" that would "permit the award of multiple licences with exclusivity periods determined by the responsible minister" and remove the "'no less favourable' industry funding requirement" for the wagering and betting licence, arguing this would "maximise the value of the licence to the state." The member for Thomastown supported the bill, noting it was "quite narrow" and about "making sure that legislation has adapted and responded to the changing nature of society," while acknowledging gambling harm and the need for balance with recreation and jobs.

Opposition members were more critical, particularly of process and consultation. The member for Gippsland East argued the government "cannot make a raft of changes that impact on the bottom line" of pubs and clubs so soon after negotiating 20-year electronic gaming machine arrangements, calling it a "sovereign risk issue." The member for Gippsland South's amendment sought an exemption from mandatory 4 am to 10 am closure periods for venues competing with Crown Casino, a change the member for Gippsland East supported, noting the casino was exempt despite the government "spruiking its strongest casino laws in the world." The member for Eildon raised concerns about "intellectual property that Tabcorp currently holds," including customer data and odds, and criticised the government for not fully explaining arrangements around multiple licences or the confidential memorandum of understanding with the racing industry. The member for Box Hill, speaking on the related **Gambling and Liquor Legislation Amendment Bill 2022**, noted that "industry and the various stakeholders who have an interest in this bill were not consulted before it landed in the house," which he called "quite unusual."

Debate also covered the **Gambling Regulation Amendment (Wagering and Betting Tax) Bill 2021**, which was guillotined at 7 pm on 20 May 2021 under a government business program motion moved by the Leader of the House, with opposition cooperation acknowledged. In South Australia, the Minister for Consumer and Business Affairs advised that the Liquor and Gambling Commissioner had appointed former Supreme Court Justice Brian Ross Martin to investigate "the suitability of SkyCity Adelaide Pty Ltd to hold the South Australian casino licence," following AUSTRAC investigations into alleged breaches of anti-money laundering laws. The minister noted the commissioner's review was "much broader than the current AUSTRAC enforcement investigation" and included analysis of facial recognition data and probity records.

lede.text:
Parliament argued sharply over mandatory carded play and precommitment on poker machines, with Labor backing "landmark gambling reforms" while the Liberal–Nationals claimed they infringed personal freedoms and would cost pub and club jobs. Greyhound racing bans drew fierce support, with Emma Hurst arguing cruelty was "built into" the industry's business model, against defenders citing regional importance.

From 1993 to 2009 parliament fought over banning online gambling as hypocritical and unworkable. In 2016–18 NSW banned then repealed greyhound racing and set a 10 per cent point-of-consumption tax. From 2020 Victoria pursued licensing, taxation and harm-minimisation reform. Attention has risen, now centring on carded play, cashless controls and racing bans.

Sixty-nine per cent of Australians believed they saw too many betting advertisements in 2025. Pokie losses reached $3.03 billion in Victoria in 2023–24. Labor, Liberal, Nationals and Greens all support the gambling reform bill; Andrew Wilkie notes poker machines fall to the states.
